newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Slain Peru rebel leader wrote to son before dying.
newsitem.headline: Slain Peru rebel leader wrote to son before dying.

text.p: Peruvian rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini told his son in a letter shortly before dying that the attack on the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima was the only way to release his mother from prison so they could be reunited.
"You need her by your side and there is no other way of getting her out of jail," Cerpa said in the note, dated April 13, which was published on Tuesday by the local daily Clarin.

Cerpa's wife, Nancy Gilvonio, is serving a life sentence for taking part in a 1995 rebel action and was among 450 prisoners whose release Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement rebels sought when they stormed the residence in December.
The siege ended last week with the deaths of 14 rebels and the release alive of all but one of 72 hostages.
The letter to 10-year-old Nestor Cerpa was faxed to a correspondent of Clarin in Lima by the boy's grandmother, Felicitas.

"My dear little dwarf...I am well and resolute. I have always told you that solidarity is the greatest virtue of man, and I want to show solidarity with my colleagues in prison and especially with your mommy. By doing so I am showing solidarity with you (and your younger brother)...because, like me, you both need her very very much", Cerpa told his son.

"It is also true that there are families of those who are being held here by us who are also suffering, but one day they will have to understand that there are children like you who also suffer, and so the wounds will heal."

He also thanked his son, whom he referred to as "my little bear" and "my remembered child," for writing a letter to Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a mediator in the hostage crisis, who he said was "doing everything humanly possible to search for a good outcome."

"Keep trusting me. I will never let you down. And if I ever leave this Japanese residence it will be because I achieved what you are waiting for and dreaming of: having your mommy outside prison, being able again to see her, touch her, play with her and be surrounded by her arms."
Cerpa was shot dead in the dramatic raid carried out a week ago by Peruvian commandos on the Japanese residence.
Ironically, Cerpa also told his son in the letter that while Peru's national soccer team was doing badly, the rebels were enjoying their own indoor tournament.
"We have a small improvised pitch and your dad is remembering the good times," Cerpa said.
When troops blasted into the residence through a hole in the floor last week, 10 of the rebels were playing soccer and several were killed on the spot.

Cerpa's wife is in the same maximun security prison in Yanamayo, southern Peru, as American Lori Berenson, who was also sentenced to life imprisonment in 1996 for treason and being a leader of the MRTA. Berenson expressed sympathy for the MRTA but rejected charges of participating in guerrilla activity.
